question.worked_solution:
Recall that a linear congruence $ax≡b\,(\text{mod}\,n)$ has a unique solution modulo $n$ if and only if $\text{gcd}(a,n)=1.$ 

In the given congruence, we have $a=17$ and $n=50$, where

$$
\text{gcd}(a,n)=\text{gcd}(17,50)=1.
$$

So, our congruence does indeed have a unique solution.

To find the solution, we need to multiply both sides of the equation by the multiplicative inverse of $17\,(\text{mod}\,50).$ To find the inverse of $17\,(\text{mod}\,50)$, use the extended Euclidean algorithm.

First, we apply the forward reduction:  

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}50 & = & 17\cdot 2 & + & 16 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 17 & = & 16\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}16 & =50-17\cdot 2 \\ 1 & =17-16\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =17-16 \\  & =17-(50-17\cdot 2) \\  & =17\cdot 3-50\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result in modulo $50,$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}17\cdot 3-50 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 17\cdot 3 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,50)\end{aligned}
$$

So, $17\cdot 3≡1\,(\text{mod}\,50),$ which means that $3$ is the multiplicative inverse of $17$ (modulo $50$).

Now, multiplying both sides of our original congruence by $3,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}17x & ≡9 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 3\cdot 17x & ≡3\cdot 9 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ (3\cdot 17)x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ 1\cdot x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50) \\ x & ≡27 &  & (\text{mod}\,50)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x≡27\,(\text{mod}\,50).$
